summary: The EST protocol defines the /.well-known/est URI and a set of path components used for certificate enrollment and other PKI services. This document defines a number of other path components that clients can use for more services.

plainLanguage.summary: EST is a service for getting digital ID cards for devices. This adds more counters at the same service window for other tasks.

questions: what is the est package availability list
subtitle: New EST path components that let a PKI server hand a device its certificates, keys, firmware and trust anchors, guided by a package list.

tldr.problem: EST (RFC 7030) covers certificate enrollment, but a device that has just enrolled also needs peer certificates, revocation lists, keys, firmware and trust anchors to operate securely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds six path components under /.well-known/est: /pal, /eecerts, /crls, /symmetrickeys, /firmware and /tamp. It extends /serverkeygen too. The /pal list tells a client which packages to fetch or return.
tldr.outcome: A server can push everything a client needs after enrollment through one familiar HTTP and TLS service. Support for the PAL itself is optional.

today: RFC 8295 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7030.

sections.title: What EST Extensions Add
sections.content:
The EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport) protocol in RFC 7030 defines the Well-Known URI /.well-known/est and path components (PCs) such as /simpleenroll and /simplereenroll. A server that wants to offer more PKI-related services can reuse the same URI by defining more path components. This document defines six:

  • /pal: the Package Availability List, a list of packages available and authorized for a client.
  • /eecerts: end-entity certificates of the client's peers.
  • /crls: certificate and authority revocation lists.
  • /symmetrickeys and /symmetrickeys/return: symmetric keys, plus receipts and errors.
  • /firmware and /firmware/return: firmware and software updates, plus receipts and errors.
  • /tamp and /tamp/return: trust anchor management packages and the client's answers.

It also extends /serverkeygen from RFC 7030. The motivation is to give clients packages during enrollment so they can perform securely afterwards, though the services can be used after enrollment as well.

Authentication, authorization, TLS cipher suites and server URI configuration all follow RFC 7030. Everything is a package, an object holding one or more content types. Packages are signed by their creator and wrapped in CMS signed-data, except certificates and CRLs, which a CA has already signed.
sections.plainLanguage: EST is the front desk for device ID cards. This RFC opens six more windows at the same desk: one for a checklist, and others for contacts' cards, cancelled-card lists, secret keys, software updates and the list of who to trust.

sections.title: The Package Availability List
sections.content:
The PAL is an XML or JSON object served from /pal. It advertises packages the client can retrieve, notifies the client to begin certificate management or to return receipts and errors, and can point to another PAL. A client asks with an HTTP GET and sets the Accept header to application/xml or application/json. The server answers with a 200 response in the matching content type.

Each entry has four fields:

  • type: a 4-digit package type string. It is required.
  • date: when the client last downloaded that package, as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ. It is omitted if there was no download or the entry is a pointer or a request to the client.
  • size: package size in bytes. It is required, and zero means the client must start a transaction or return an error or receipt.
  • info: exactly one of a DN, an SKI, an issuer and serial number, or a URI where the package can be fetched.

Clients may be limited in the size of objects they can handle, so package type 0001 says that another PAL is available. If present it MUST be the last entry, and it MUST NOT be the only entry.

When building a PAL the server orders entries by importance: /cacerts and /crls first, then /csrattrs, then enrollment (/simpleenroll, /simplereenroll, /fullcmc), and finally /symmetrickeys, /firmware, /tamp and /eecerts. Packages the client has not downloaded before SHOULD get precedence. Support for the PAL is OPTIONAL, and a client does not need it to use the other services. Both sides MUST authenticate each other and check authorization as RFC 7030 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: The PAL is a to-do list from the server. Each line says what kind of thing to pick up, how big it is and where to find it, and the most important things come first.

sections.title: PAL Package Types
sections.content:
Package types are hints about what a client is about to fetch or is asked to return. They do not replace the client's duty to check what it actually receives before storing it. Types 0000 to 0037 are defined, and 0000 is reserved. They fall into groups:

  • 0002 to 0005: CA certificates, EE certificates, ARLs and CRLs.
  • 0006 to 0019: starting, completing or failing enrollment and re-enrollment for digital signature (DS) and key establishment (KE) certificates.
  • 0020 to 0023: asymmetric key packages in PKCS #8, CMS or PKCS #12 form, and their receipt or error.
  • 0024 to 0027: symmetric key and firmware packages, and their receipts or errors.
  • 0028 to 0037: TAMP queries, updates and their confirmations or errors.

An entry for a thing the server wants back, such as a receipt, points to a /return URI. Placing such an entry after the entries for retrieving the packages is the same as requesting receipts in the originally distributed package. The semantics of types 0002 and 0006 to 0021 come from RFC 7030.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line on the to-do list has a number that tells you what kind of job it is, like pick up a card, sign a form or send back a thank-you note.

sections.title: Certificates, Revocation Lists and Keys
sections.content:
Certificates and CRLs. /eecerts is not a general repository. It is a push mechanism for peer certificates that the server knows, out of band, the client will talk to. For example, a router with two peers can be given their certificates along with its own. /crls similarly delivers CRLs and ARLs so the client need not parse a certificate to discover where to fetch them. Both use an HTTP GET and return a certs-only or crls-only message. The server need not authenticate or authorize the client, since a CA has already signed the contents. The client MUST reject anything that does not validate to an authorized trust anchor.

Symmetric keys. A client GETs /symmetrickeys and receives a 200 response of type application/cms holding a symmetric key package. By default the key is protected only by the TLS cipher suite, so that suite MUST be commensurate in strength with the key and MUST NOT use NULL encryption. The RFC strongly recommends that servers always return encrypted keys. Extra layers (enveloped-data, nested signed-data, or an encrypted key package when CMS Content Constraints are supported) are optional.

Asymmetric keys. /serverkeygen is extended with more CMS content types, a /serverkeygen/return path for receipts and errors, and PKCS #12 delivery. For PKCS #12 the client POSTs a CSR, and the server MUST ignore the public key and signature in it. The response is application/pkcs12, and the private key and certificate arrive in one PFX. Password-based encryption of that file is supported, and distributing the password is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can hand over useful things in advance, like the ID cards of people you will meet, lists of cancelled cards and secret codes. Secret codes need a strong lock while they travel.

sections.title: Firmware, Trust Anchors and Receipts
sections.content:
Firmware. For devices that cannot update themselves, /firmware lets the infrastructure announce firmware and software updates. The client GETs it and receives application/cms content: the bare firmware package, compressed data, encrypted-data, or signed-data wrapping any of those. A signed package MUST be rejected if the signature does not validate to an authorized trust anchor.

Trust anchors. The /tamp path component carries Trust Anchor Management Protocol packages from RFC 5934: status query, trust anchor update, apex trust anchor update, community update and sequence number adjust. Each has its own media type, such as application/tamp-update. TAMP lets a device add or replace roots without a new software load. Clients MUST validate these packages with a certificate and reject them if the signature does not validate to an authorized trust anchor.

Receipts and errors. Each service has a /return companion that a client POSTs to. It reports a receipt or error for the package it handled: /symmetrickeys/return, /firmware/return, /tamp/return and /serverkeygen/return. Clients can be configured to send them automatically, to respond to a receipt-request attribute, or to send them when a PAL entry asks. A successful return gets a 204 response with no content. Rejections use an HTTP 4xx or 5xx status.
sections.plainLanguage: After picking up a package, the device mails back a note saying whether it worked. The server can also send software updates and a new list of who to trust.

sections.title: PAL and Certificate Enrollment
sections.content:
When a client enrolls, it normally POSTs a request and receives a certificate or a CMC response, as described for /simpleenroll, /simplereenroll and /fullcmc in RFC 7030. With the PAL, the client first pulls the PAL, finds a package type that starts enrollment, and then proceeds as usual. It can also begin enrollment assisted by a CSR attributes template from /csrattrs.

The PAL also helps recovery. If a server closes the connection early, or a client cannot stay connected for the whole enrollment, the client does not know whether its request was processed. It can reconnect, authenticate the server again, download the PAL, and use the entry to fetch the success or failure response with an HTTP GET to the enrollment path.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone call drops while you are applying for an ID card, you can call back, read the checklist, and find out whether your application went through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC relies on many other specifications, and all the security considerations of RFC 7030 apply. It points to the specifications for HTTP, HTTPS and TLS, URIs, the content types, the algorithms that protect packages, random numbers and server-generated key pairs.

Two notes in the text are worth knowing. A signature check on symmetric or asymmetric key packages is only a sanity check unless the client has a policy requiring a signature, because a malicious EST server could simply strip the signature. And the symmetric key default relies on the TLS cipher suite, so a NULL-encryption suite would expose the key.
sections.plainLanguage: A thief who controls the front desk could remove the signature stamp, so the device should insist on one. Secret codes must never be sent in the open.
